synopsis: Ava DuVernay traces a line from the Thirteenth Amendment's prison-labour loophole to modern American mass incarceration, building the case through archive footage and interviews with historians, activists and politicians. The argument is marshalled rather than balanced, and it is the editing - cuts that set rhetoric beside its consequences - that lands hardest.

A bicycle courier wakes from a coma in a London emptied by a rage virus and joins a handful of survivors driving north towards a military broadcast promising safety. Shot on consumer digital video, which makes the deserted city feel found rather than built, and the soldiers scarier than the infected.

In Ceaușescu's Romania, a student spends one long day arranging an illegal abortion for her flatmate, haggling in hotel corridors with a man who sets his own price. Mungiu holds each scene in a single unbroken take, so the dread accumulates in real time rather than arriving.

A celebrated director with a production already in motion and nothing to shoot hides out at a spa, where memories, fantasies and everyone owed a decision crowd in on him. Fellini turns creative paralysis into spectacle, and more or less invented the genre of film about not being able to make the film.

An RAF pilot bails out without a parachute, survives, and is told by a heavenly emissary that his reprieve was a clerical error to be argued before a celestial court. The afterlife is monochrome and Earth is Technicolor, a joke about post-war Anglo-American relations that still lands.

Two mismatched American cousins take a Holocaust heritage tour of Poland, one tightly wound and the other charming, exhausting and impossible to be around for long. Eisenberg writes himself the thankless part and hands Culkin the fireworks, which is the film's quiet act of generosity.

Years after bullying a deaf classmate out of his primary school, a teenager tracks her down, having taught himself sign language and having no idea what he wants from her. Unusually willing to sit with the possibility that an apology is mostly for the person making it.

A thirteen-year-old boy is arrested for the murder of a girl from his school, and the fallout plays out across four episodes, each filmed in one continuous unbroken take. The technique could have been a stunt; instead it traps you in rooms with people who cannot leave either.

Food poisoning takes out the flight crew, leaving a traumatised ex-fighter pilot to land the plane while the ground controllers dispense increasingly unhelpful advice. Built by playing a 1957 disaster script entirely straight and packing every corner of the frame with gags; the density is the whole method.

An adoring young fan is taken up by an ageing Broadway star and begins, politely and methodically, to take over her life. Mankiewicz gives everyone lines nobody could improvise and the theatre setting excuses it, which is how the cruelty stays funny for well over two hours.

After her teenage son is killed on his birthday, a Madrid nurse goes back to Barcelona to find his father and falls in with a trans sex worker, a pregnant nun and a stage actress. Almodóvar's warmest film about grief, built entirely from women holding each other up.

A Chinese glass billionaire reopens a shuttered General Motors plant in Ohio, and the camera follows both the American workers and the Chinese managers flown in to fix them. Shot with remarkable access over several years, and refreshingly unwilling to hand either side the role of villain.

Three Mexico City lives collide in one car crash: a boy running dogfights for money, a model trapped in a half-furnished flat, and a homeless assassin who was once a guerrilla. Iñárritu's debut, and the one where the triptych structure feels discovered rather than assembled.

Assembled entirely from home video, voicemails and paparazzi footage, this traces Amy Winehouse from a funny north London teenager to a woman photographed to death. Kapadia films no talking heads at all, and the absence of hindsight makes it feel like watching it happen again.

A Brooklyn stripper marries the reckless son of a Russian oligarch on impulse, and his parents send three men to undo it before word reaches Moscow. Baker lets a screwball chase run for an hour, then removes the comedy so quietly you barely notice him doing it.

Four bored Danish schoolteachers test a theory that people function better with a permanent low level of alcohol in the blood, and keep careful notes as the experiment escalates. Neither a cautionary tale nor a celebration, which is exactly why the last scene is so hard to read.

Built from large-format footage and thousands of hours of mission audio found unlogged in government archives, this follows the 1969 landing with no narration, no interviews and no reenactment. The 70mm images of the launch-day crowd are as startling as anything that happens in space.

In a gilded city built on top of a poisoned undercity, two sisters separated by a childhood catastrophe end up on opposite sides of a coming war over magic and industry. Adapted from a video game yet written as family tragedy, and the painted animation has no real peer on television.

A young woman in a Dakar suburb is promised to a rich man while the boy she loves takes a boat for Spain with a crew of unpaid builders, and then odd things start happening at night. Diop films a migration story as a ghost story, and the genre shift is the argument.

Humanity shelters behind enormous walls until giant humanoids breach them, and a boy who watched his mother die enlists in the corps that fights back. Begins as siege horror and turns steadily into a study of how atrocity gets inherited; the mid-series reveals reframe almost everything that came before them.

The last of the air nomads, a twelve-year-old monk, is thawed out of an iceberg a hundred years into a war of conquest, and is the only person alive able to bend all four elements. Serialised for children who were trusted with genocide, occupation and a redemption arc that takes three years.

Sixteen years after the original, the BBC returns to the oceans with suction-cam rigs, low-light cameras and submersibles reaching trenches never filmed before, one habitat per episode. Attenborough narrates, and the closing turn towards plastic shifted British policy, which wildlife television almost never manages.

Two high-achieving best friends discover on the eve of graduation that the classmates they looked down on got into the same universities anyway, and set out to salvage one night of fun. Structurally a familiar teen comedy, but the friendship is written with real specificity and the jokes land.

Broke and adrift after her bakery folds, a woman is made maid of honour by her oldest friend and finds herself outmanoeuvred at every stage by a richer, smoother rival bridesmaid. Wiig and Mumolo write humiliation rather than raunch, which is why it holds up better than its imitators.

A married suburban woman and a married doctor meet by chance in a railway station tea room and fall into an affair conducted almost entirely in words. Rachmaninov underneath and clipped middle-class diction on top; the restraint is the thing that hurts, and it was engineered to.

Two detectives who dislike each other work the death of a boy found beneath the cliffs of a small Dorset town, while the town starts tearing at itself and the press arrives. The first series is near-perfect procedural television; the later ones never quite recover the trick.

Running out of room in a West that is closing behind them, two charming train robbers are pursued by a posse that will not give up and light out for Bolivia with a schoolteacher in tow. Goldman's script more or less invented the modern buddy film, banter and melancholy in the same breath.

In Weimar Berlin, an American singer at a shabby nightclub takes up with an English student while the Nazis move from a street joke to the thing everybody is careful about. Fosse keeps every song inside the club, so the numbers comment on the story instead of interrupting it.

A sheltered, bullied teenager raised by a religious fanatic discovers she can move objects with her mind, just as the cruellest girls at school arrange an apology she cannot see through. De Palma's split screens and slow motion turn a school prom into something close to opera.

Losing badly on the minor circuit, a tennis pro is entered by his wife and coach into a low-tier tournament where his opponent turns out to be the man they both knew before everything went wrong. Guadagnino cuts the matches like sex scenes and the sex scenes like matches.

A successful filmmaker learns that the projectionist who taught him as a boy in a Sicilian village has died, and remembers the fleapit cinema where he grew up. Sentimental by design, but unusually clear-eyed about what leaving home costs; the shorter international cut is the more disciplined film of the two.

Poitras films Edward Snowden in a Hong Kong hotel room across eight days in June 2013 as he hands NSA documents to journalists and waits to be identified by name. Because she was one of the contacts he chose, the camera sits inside the story rather than reconstructing it afterwards.

Two thirteen-year-old boys in the Belgian flower fields are inseparable until schoolyard teasing about their closeness makes one of them pull away. Dhont films adolescent shame at unbearable proximity, and the second half rests almost entirely on a child actor carrying grief he has no words for.

A rich, relentlessly capable Beverly Hills teenager takes on a new girl as a makeover project while missing everything about her own love life. Heckerling's transplant of Jane Austen's Emma into Valley slang is sharper than its reputation, and the satire likes its heroine rather than sneering at her.

A pianist and a singer meet in a post-war Polish folk ensemble and spend fifteen years crossing the Iron Curtain towards and away from each other. Pawlikowski compresses a doomed affair into eighty-nine minutes of boxy black-and-white, cutting away from scenes just before they resolve.

The Pope dies, and the cardinal charged with running the election discovers that every leading candidate is carrying something he would rather keep buried. Procedure as thriller — ballots, robes and whispered lobbying, played mostly on Fiennes's face, with a closing turn that will split any room watching it.

A bounty-hunter crew drift around a terraformed solar system in a beaten-up ship, chasing small paydays while their separate pasts close in. Watanabe scores noir, westerns and kung fu to live jazz, and the throwaway episodic gigs quietly assemble one of the sadder arcs in television animation.

An East German border guard is press-ganged into spying on the West and planted as an aide to a Bundeswehr general at the height of the Able Archer scare. Cold War paranoia played with pop music and real wit; the tradecraft is amateurish on purpose, and better for it.

After their daughter drowns, a married couple take restoration work in a wintry Venice where a blind psychic insists the child is trying to reach them. Roeg splices past, present and premonition until grief and foresight become the same thing, and the famous love scene still startles.

An American general goes rogue and orders a nuclear strike, leaving a war room full of men to talk their way out of the end of the world. Kubrick shoots it as a straight thriller and lets Sellers play three roles; the horror is that every procedure works exactly as designed.

The heir to a ducal house is moved to a desert planet his family cannot hold, where the only export worth killing for lies under the sand. Villeneuve trades pulp for scale and dread, and it is unashamedly half a story — the ending simply stops.

A man returns to a cabin in the woods, plays a recording of an ancient text, and spends the night fighting demons, the furniture and his own right hand. Raimi remakes his own film as slapstick, with a camera that behaves like a cartoon and Campbell taking every beating going.

A French shop owner spends years filming street artists, proves incapable of cutting the footage into anything, and reinvents himself as an artist instead. Banksy took the tapes and assembled this: a film about art-market hype that never once confirms how much of itself was set up.

Two boys trained brutally in a Peking opera school become stars playing king and concubine, and their offstage bond is ground down by fifty years of Chinese upheaval. Chen stages history as backstage melodrama, and Leslie Cheung carries a longing the film never has to state aloud.

A married pair of French volcanologists spent twenty years filming eruptions from close enough to be killed by them, and this is built almost entirely from the 16mm footage they left behind. Dosa cuts their own images into a love story; the arch, whimsical narration will divide people.

An Afghan refugee, now an academic in Denmark, tells a friend the full story of his escape for the first time, animated so that he can tell it without being identified. The animation does real work here, wobbling into abstraction whenever the memory becomes unbearable.

A cat is driven from its home by a rising flood and ends up sharing a boat with a capybara, a lemur, a dog and a secretarybird, none of whom speak. Zilbalodis made it in free software on a tiny budget with no dialogue at all, and the animal behaviour is observed rather than cartooned.

A Swedish family at a French ski resort watch an avalanche roll towards their terrace, and the father's split-second reaction poisons the rest of the holiday. Östlund holds shots long past comfort, turning one instinct into days of marital cross-examination that are funnier and crueller than that sounds.

At four weddings and one funeral, a chronically single Londoner keeps running into the same American woman and keeps failing to say anything useful about it. Curtis's script gave Britain a decade of romantic-comedy exports, and the funeral in the middle is why it still holds up.

A climber prepares to go up El Capitan's 900-metre face without ropes, while the crew filming him work out where to stand so they do not distract him into falling. It is as much about the girlfriend and the cameramen as the route, which is the only thing that makes the ascent watchable.

Two brothers maim themselves in a forbidden attempt to bring their mother back, then join a state alchemy programme to find a way of restoring their bodies. This is the version that follows the manga all the way to its end, and its sixty-four episodes plan their payoffs years in advance.

Reporters are invited to the reopened resort where android hosts once killed the guests, and find the new management rather too eager to show them everything. The Westworld sequel is talkier and cheaper than the original, though the delirious dream sequence with Brynner is worth the detour.

Months of flirting over the phone at work bring an Essex lad and a Barry girl together fast, dragging two very different families into permanent contact. The couple are really the pretext; the comedy lives with the friends and parents around them, Smithy and Nessa above all.

A London gangster goes home to Newcastle to bury his brother, refuses to accept the accident story, and works his way up the local trade one conversation at a time. Hodges shoots the north as cold and unglamorous, and Caine plays a man with no charm left in him at all.

In a drowned, neon-lit future city, a cyborg security agent hunts a hacker who breaks into people's minds, and the case keeps circling back to whether anything of hers is still her own. Oshii stops the plot dead for long wordless passages; the philosophy is stated flatly, the images do the persuading.

A pilot who failed to fly his kamikaze mission returns to a flattened Tokyo carrying the shame, then faces a creature the defeated country has no army left to fight. Yamazaki puts the human melodrama first and spends his small budget only where it shows; the monster is frightening again.

Clans on the outskirts of Naples run cocaine, construction and public housing as a business, and the series follows a boss, his wife, his lieutenant and the teenagers coming up beneath them. Bleak and unglamorous as a matter of policy - nobody gets a redemption arc, and the dialect is subtitled even in Italy.

For thirteen summers a self-appointed bear protector lived among Alaskan grizzlies and filmed himself doing it, until they killed him; Herzog cuts a hundred hours of that footage into this. The film is an argument between his sentimental view of nature and Herzog's, and it is scrupulous about what it refuses to show.

A contemptuous weatherman sent to cover a small-town festival wakes to the same day again, and again, with no explanation offered and no way out. What begins as a gag engine turns into a serious film about unlimited time, and Murray's souring and recovery is the whole architecture.

Two stepbrothers thrown together by childhood tragedy are pulled back into each other's lives when one turns up uninvited at the other's wedding and the night ends in violence. Gadd's follow-up to Baby Reindeer then works backwards through three decades; it is about male rage, and it is not an easy watch.

A man who killed his sister as a child escapes the institution fifteen years later and walks back to the same Illinois town, where a teenage babysitter is the only person paying attention. Carpenter builds the dread almost entirely out of empty widescreen space and his own synthesiser score.

In Stratford, a glovemaker's son marries a woman the town thinks strange and leaves for London to write, and their eleven-year-old son dies of plague while he is away. Zhao stays with the mother rather than the playwright, and the final stretch, set in a theatre, does what a novel can only describe.

After her secretive mother dies, a miniature artist watches her family come apart through grief, a teenage son's guilt and something older working underneath it. Aster builds dread out of domestic detail and Collette's performance; the final twenty minutes divide people, but the ninety before them are close to flawless.

Two teenagers from Chicago's West Side are recruited by a suburban basketball powerhouse, and the crew keeps filming for five years as injuries, scholarship money and family finances reshape both lives. Cut from hundreds of hours of footage into something closer to a novel than a sports film.

A London officer too good for his own force is exiled to a spotless West Country village where the accident rate is suspiciously high. Wright turns a parish of swans and village-of-the-year committees into a genuine action film, and the joke is always on the genre rather than the locals.

An amateur cyclist sets out to dope himself through a gruelling race to prove the testing system can be beaten, then discovers his Russian scientific adviser runs Moscow's state doping programme and needs to get out of the country. The film changes subject mid-shoot, and that swerve is its strongest argument.

In 1962 Poland, a novice about to take her vows is sent to meet the only relative she has left, a hard-drinking state judge who tells her she is Jewish and that her parents lie in an unmarked grave. Shot in boxy black-and-white with heads pushed low in the frame, the empty space doing the grieving.

A disgraced television presenter hosts the graveyard shift on Radio Norwich, lives in a roadside travel tavern and pitches doomed formats to broadcasters who will not return his calls. Comedy of pure social agony, and Coogan commits to the flinching so completely that the silences do most of the work.

Rio, 1971: plain-clothes officers take a former congressman from his house, and his wife spends the decades that follow refusing the state's silence about what became of him. Torres plays composure rather than collapse, which makes the politics land harder than any speech would.

Every episode is a self-contained half-hour set behind a door numbered nine: a wardrobe, a village hall, a call centre, a sleeper carriage, each with a trick in its construction. Pemberton and Shearsmith write the lot, and the range is the point, since some are cruel jokes and some are quiet tragedies.

After a sexual encounter, a teenager is told she has been passed something that will walk towards her, slowly and forever, wearing any face it likes. Mitchell shoots the emptied-out Detroit suburbs in wide, patient frames so you scan the background yourself, which beats any jump scare.

Christmas Eve finds a small-town building-and-loan manager, who gave up every plan he ever had for other people, at the end of his rope - until he is shown what the town would have become without him. Far darker than its reputation as festive comfort viewing suggests, because the despair is played straight.

A ten-year-old in the Hitler Youth, coached by an imaginary buffoon of a Fuhrer, finds his mother is hiding a Jewish girl behind the attic wall. The satire is broad by design, and the film works because the gags keep getting interrupted by consequences.

Two friends, one Austrian and one French, love the same restless woman across two decades and a war that puts them in opposing armies. Truffaut's camera moves as though improvising, though the film is far colder about its heroine than its reputation as a great romance suggests.

A bullied Barnsley boy with no prospects at school or at home takes a kestrel from a nest and teaches himself falconry out of a stolen library book. Loach casts non-professionals and lets scenes run, so the classroom and the pit-town streets play like documentary, and the ending is administered rather than dramatised.

The disinherited son of a duke's daughter works his way through the eight relatives standing between him and the family title, narrating each removal with impeccable manners. Guinness plays all eight victims, but the film belongs to Price's icy voiceover and to one of the great closing beats in British comedy.

A pampered postmaster's son is posted to a frozen island town whose two clans have feuded for generations, and strikes a bargain with a reclusive toymaker living out in the woods. Hand-drawn with lighting that makes flat animation look sculpted, and it earns its sentiment instead of assuming it.

A chart-topping girl group moonlight as demon hunters guarding the barrier between worlds, then find that their new rivals, a boy band with suspiciously devoted fans, are the thing they are supposed to be fighting. The songs carry the plot rather than decorate it, and the animation takes its timing from music video.

In an 1893 village crushed by colonial land tax, a young farmer accepts a British officer's wager: beat the cantonment at cricket and the tax is cancelled for three years. Three and a half hours that never drag, with the match staged as an anti-colonial set piece rather than a sports finale.

In a snowbound Stockholm housing estate, a bullied twelve-year-old befriends the strange child who has moved in next door, who appears only after dark and whose guardian kills on her behalf. Alfredson shoots the horror flat and distant, so the tenderness and the predation share the same frame.

A Houston oil executive is sent to buy a Scottish coastal village for a refinery and finds the locals far keener to sell than he is to buy. Forsyth lets the comedy drift rather than build, and it closes on an ache most comedies never reach for.

Colonists bound for a new world crash-land on an unmapped planet, one family cut off from their ship and stuck with an alien machine and a con artist travelling under a stolen name. Handsome, competent family science fiction that solves a fresh engineering crisis each week; the peril resets often enough to blunt it.

A reclusive puzzle-setter impersonates his missing identical twin, a detective inspector, and ends up closing murder cases by logic while quietly hunting for the man he is pretending to be. Mitchell's deadpan carries it, and the series is warmer about grief and marriage than the high-concept premise implies.

Exonerated by DNA after eighteen years inside, a Wisconsin man is arrested for a murder two years later, and the filmmakers follow his trial and his young nephew's disputed confession across a decade. Built from trial footage and prison phone calls; gripping, though it argues a case rather than testing one.

A French wire-walker and a scratch crew smuggle cable and rigging into the World Trade Center overnight in August 1974, planning to string a line between the towers before dawn. Marsh tells it as a heist, with reconstructions and participants still giddy on camera, and never once mentions what the buildings later became.

Eight thieves who take the names of cities seal themselves inside the Royal Mint of Spain to print their own ransom, while a man calling himself the Professor runs the negotiation from outside. The plotting is absurd and the flashbacks repetitive, but the hostage chess and the cast's conviction carry it.

A single mother becomes convinced her son's teacher is hurting him and the school stonewalls her, after which the same few days replay from two other points of view. Kore-eda's structure is the argument: each retelling shows how confidently adults misread children.

Arthur and his knights ride coconut-shell horses across a muddy, underfunded Britain in search of the grail, delayed by French taunts, a killer rabbit and a great deal of arguing about political theory. Cheap by necessity, which is why it still looks like nothing else; the sketch structure means the hit rate varies.

A man born in the stable next door to Jesus is repeatedly mistaken for the messiah, acquiring followers he never wanted along with the attention of Rome and several rival liberation fronts. The Pythons' most structured film, and its sharpest material is about factionalism rather than religion.

A burned-out filmmaker starts free-diving every day in a Cape kelp forest and spends a year following one common octopus, who slowly stops hiding from him. The underwater footage is extraordinary; the narration insists on the friendship rather than trusting you to see it.

Two dozen singers, hangers-on and hopefuls circle the country-music capital over five days while a political operative books stars for a populist candidate's rally. Altman's overlapping sound mix leaves you to choose what to listen to, and the songs are written and performed by the actors themselves.

A camera crew sits with the Russian opposition leader in Germany as he recovers from Novichok poisoning and, working with open-source investigators, telephones the men who tried to kill him. The call is astonishing footage, though the film is closer to campaign portrait than inquiry and hurries past his nationalist past.

Teenagers are conscripted to pilot enormous biomechanical units against the creatures attacking the last fortified city, commanded by a father who treats his son as equipment. Begins as a mecha show and ends as a study of depression and self-loathing, with a late budget collapse that hardened into a style.

Two boys at a segregated Florida reform school in the early 1960s survive its beatings and disappearances by opposite strategies, one hopeful and one watchful. Shot almost entirely from inside their eyelines, a formal risk that makes the friendship, rather than the brutality, the thing you remember.

A Palestinian activist films the slow demolition of his West Bank community over several years, and the Israeli journalist who keeps turning up becomes his collaborator and the film's uneasy second subject. Made by a four-person Palestinian-Israeli collective, and the friction between the two men is what lifts it above reportage.

Bond, five years retired in Jamaica, is pulled back by an old CIA friend and a stolen bioweapon that kills on contact with a target's DNA. Craig's era signs off by letting the character carry consequences at last; the plot creaks under its own length, the farewell doesn't.

In 1830s Germany an ancient count fixes on a young wife from a distance, and has her estate-agent husband summoned to a Carpathian castle to close a property sale. Eggers rebuilds the 1922 original as sickly, candlelit period horror - more oppressive than frightening, with a deliberately unlovely vampire.

An ex-prizefighter working the New York docks under a mob-run longshoremen's union is pushed to testify after he helps set up a murder. Kazan made it partly to justify naming names to HUAC, which gives its moral argument an uncomfortable double life and a strange power.

A convoy of policemen, a prosecutor and a doctor drive a confessed killer around the Anatolian steppe at night, hunting for a body he cannot quite remember burying. Nearly three hours of headlights, small talk and waiting that turn out to be about guilt rather than procedure.

Sixteen years after his revolutionary cell scattered, a burnt-out ex-militant living under a false name has to find his teenage daughter when the army colonel he once tangled with resurfaces. Anderson plays paranoia for farce as much as dread, and the chase over the rolling desert road is superbly cut.

Two brothers run a market-trading business out of a Peckham tower block, always one dodgy consignment away from the fortune they have been promising each other for years. The catchphrases obscure how carefully it is built — the famous pratfalls land because the class disappointment under them is real.

A small bear from Peru takes odd jobs to buy his aunt a pop-up book for her birthday, and ends up in prison for the theft of it. Sweetness engineered with real rigour, and Hugh Grant's vain, washed-up actor is the funniest thing in either film.

In a Bengali village, a family scrape by on a father's unpaid poetry and unreliable work, seen mostly through the eyes of a small boy and his restless older sister. Ray shot it at weekends with an almost entirely inexperienced crew, and the improvisation reads as attentiveness rather than roughness.

A girl grows up in Tehran through the revolution and the war with Iraq, is packed off alone to Vienna as a teenager, and returns a stranger in her own city. The stark black-and-white drawing keeps the memoir from softening into nostalgia, and the comedy stays sharp about both countries.

Six hours of wildlife filming organised by habitat — islands, mountains, jungles, deserts, grasslands and, last, cities — with Attenborough narrating. Stabilised rigs and drones put the camera inside the chase rather than beside it, which is why the racer snakes and iguana sequence is the one everybody remembers.

A misanthropic romance novelist is one of a dozen people left unchanged when a signal from space merges the rest of humanity into a single contented mind that now wants, very much, to make her happy. Gilligan swaps crime for a comedy of refusal, and Seehorn carries nearly every scene.

In 1920s Shanxi, a university student is married off as the fourth wife of a rich household where a red lantern hung outside your door announces whose bed the master has chosen tonight. The ritual is invented rather than historical, and it works as a near-perfect machine for showing the powerless policing each other.

A rat with a refined palate hides under the toque of a hopeless kitchen boy and steers him, by the hair, through service at a declining Paris restaurant. Its real subject is criticism, and the last act gives a food critic the most honest speech anyone has written about the job.

A journalist looking into her niece's death finds the cursed videotape behind it, watches it, and starts a seven-day clock on herself and her son. Cold, procedural and almost bloodless; the dread sits in television static and a covered well rather than in anything that jumps out.

Paid to sail to Italy and coax a rich man's son back to New York, a small-time forger decides he would rather have the son's life instead. Shot in cold black and white and paced like a procedural — the pleasure is watching a bad improvisation get tidied up, at length.

A European princess on a state visit slips her handlers for a day in Rome, where an American reporter recognises her and keeps that to himself while a photographer trails them. The ending is unusually unsentimental for 1953, and Hepburn's first lead role still plays like a discovery.

Newlyweds take a flat in a grand old Manhattan building with unusually attentive elderly neighbours, and the wife's pregnancy starts to feel like something being arranged around her. Almost all of the horror is social: the slow discovery that nobody, doctor or husband included, will take her seriously.

Two real Indian revolutionaries are imagined as friends in 1920s Delhi - one a tribal protector searching for a girl taken by the British governor, the other a colonial policeman who has no idea who his friend is. Physics is optional and the sincerity total; the dance-off is the restrained part.

A demoted Mumbai police officer takes a call from a gangster who tells him the city has twenty-five days left, and the gangster's life story unspools alongside the search. Two seasons split between two directors, past and present; the first is much the tighter, and Siddiqui is the engine of both.

A wealthy family lose everything to fraud and move into two adjoining motel rooms in the small town they once bought as a joke. It starts out mocking rich people and turns warm without ever staging a homophobic plot beat, which is the quiet argument underneath the whole thing.

Two South African fans set out to find what became of a Detroit folk singer whose two albums flopped in America and then, without his knowledge, soundtracked a generation under apartheid. Built from interviews and Super 8, it withholds its central fact like a thriller — and quietly omits his Australian tours to do it.

Ayrton Senna's decade in Formula One, assembled entirely from archive — race footage, onboard cameras, television interviews and the closed-door drivers' briefings where he argues with the sport's officials. No talking heads on screen, a rivalry with Prost shaped rather too neatly into drama, and cockpit footage that needs no help at all.

An estranged film director resurfaces to offer his stage-actress daughter the lead in a comeback picture about their family house and her grandmother's war; she refuses, and he casts a young American star instead. Trier writes reconciliation as something negotiated through work rather than talk, and Skarsgård plays the charm and the cowardice as one thing.

A north London shop worker whose life has stalled decides the zombie outbreak is his chance to win back his girlfriend, rescue his mum and get everyone safely to the pub. Wright's rhyming cuts and paid-off setups make it as tightly engineered as farce, and it is fonder of its characters than most comedies bother to be.

Nine and a half hours of interviews with survivors, Polish villagers and former SS men about the machinery of the extermination camps, filmed at the sites as they stood in the 1970s, with no archive footage whatsoever. Refusing reenactment and stock images makes testimony itself the evidence; the methods used on reluctant subjects are part of the argument too.

An English pilot wrecks his ship on the coast of Japan in 1600 and becomes one piece on the board of a regent manoeuvring against a council that has already condemned him. Mostly in Japanese and told from the Japanese side, which is exactly what separates it from every earlier version of the book.

A silent-film star and his studio scramble to convert a finished picture into a talkie, the leading lady's voice being the insurmountable problem. A backstage comedy about a technological panic that happens to contain the best dancing in the American musical, and the sharpest jokes about Hollywood's own history.

Seven standalone half-hours, each built around one actor alone in a room with a near-future technology: a duplicate self, transferred memories, a cryogenic sleep, an uploaded mind. An anthology designed as a monologue showcase, so it lives or dies on the writing episode by episode, and the hit rate is uneven.

Two Chicago musicians witness a gangland massacre and escape the city disguised as women in an all-female band bound for Florida. Wilder keeps the farce accelerating for two hours without a slack stretch, and closes on the best last line in American comedy.

To get a cheap north London flat advertised for professional couples only, two strangers pretend to be together, then fill the sitcom around them with film references, drink and almost no plot. Wright and Pegg's first collaboration, shot like a feature and pastiching one every week; the template for everything they made afterwards.

Pulled across the multiverse into a society of Spider-People who police it, a Brooklyn teenager learns that their rules demand a loss he refuses to accept. Every universe gets its own animation language, and the film stops mid-story rather than ending - it is openly half of one picture.

A Brooklyn teenager bitten by a spider inherits a job he does not want, and gets reluctant tutoring from a middle-aged, out-of-shape version of the hero from a neighbouring dimension. The animation runs on deliberately mismatched frame rates, halftone dots and misregistered print colour, making it the rare superhero film with a visual idea of its own.

A guide leads a writer and a scientist through a fenced-off, guarded Zone towards a room that is said to grant whatever you most deeply want. Three men arguing across ruined industrial landscapes for two and a half hours; the science fiction is the least of it, and the slowness is the method, not a flaw.

The useless son of a Greek-Cypriot letting agent blunders through viewings, tenants and office politics he only half understands, certain the family firm is owed to him. A sitcom built almost entirely on mangled speech and physical embarrassment, and far better at sudden pathos than that makes it sound.

Talking Heads play four nights at Hollywood's Pantages Theatre, the band assembling on stage one member at a time until a bare platform is a full funk orchestra. Demme almost never cuts to the audience and constantly to the players, which is why it still feels like the room rather than a souvenir.

An American ballet student arrives at a German dance academy in driving rain and finds the staff evasive, the corridors wrong and the other girls disappearing. Argento abandons plot logic for colour, tile and Goblin's score, and the film is far stranger and better for it.

A group of Australian teenagers get high on a party trick: grip an embalmed hand, invite a spirit in, and let it ride you for ninety seconds. The rules-and-timer setup gives the scares an addiction logic, and the grief underneath is handled with more care than the premise suggests.

A truck driver stops at a failing Tokyo noodle shop and stays to coach the widow who runs it towards the perfect bowl of ramen, while unrelated strangers pursue appetites of their own. The digressions are the point: a food comedy that keeps wandering off into lust, death and etiquette.

The men who carried out Indonesia's 1965 anti-communist massacres, still honoured at home, are invited to restage their killings as scenes from the Hollywood genres they love. Oppenheimer lets the boasting run until it curdles, and the method implicates the viewer nearly as much as the killers.

A junior clerk at a Manhattan insurance giant lends his flat to executives for their affairs in the hope of promotion, until he works out who the boss has been bringing there. Wilder turns corporate pimping, loneliness and a suicide attempt into the warmest comedy of its decade.

Worn down by her difficult six-year-old, a widowed mother reads him a pop-up book about a top-hatted creature that cannot be unread, and the house begins to close in. Kent shoots exhaustion and unspeakable resentment as horror, and the monster works as both real threat and diagnosis.

A twice-over lottery winner living alone on a remote island pays a fading folk singer to play a private gig, then reveals he has also booked the ex-bandmate the singer stopped speaking to years ago. Relentless chatter hides a film about grief that earns its ending without straining for it.

Three long parts cut from roughly sixty hours of 1969 studio footage, following the Beatles as they try to write and rehearse an album in three weeks with no songs and a deadline nobody believes in. Jackson's restoration is slow by design; the tedium is what makes the breakthroughs land.

A boy sent to the countryside after his mother dies in a wartime Tokyo fire follows a talking grey heron into a tower, and into the collapsing world beneath it. Miyazaki's least explicable film and probably his most personal; it works as grief logic more than as plot.

A Hungarian-Jewish architect arrives in postwar Pennsylvania with nothing and is taken up by a rich industrialist who wants a monument built, on terms that keep quietly shifting. Shot on VistaVision and built around an interval, it is about patronage as a form of ownership rather than about buildings.

In Nairobi, a mild British diplomat starts pulling at the work his murdered activist wife left behind and finds a drug trial running on Kenyan patients who were never told what they were taking. Meirelles cuts grief and investigation together until each contaminates the other; the marriage is the stronger half.

Six women descend into an unmapped cave system a year after one of them lost her family, and the passage behind them collapses. The first hour is pure claustrophobia and would work with no monster at all, which is what makes the second hour land.

A career diplomat expecting a posting to Kabul is made US ambassador to the United Kingdom instead, juggling a warship attack, a hostile Foreign Secretary and a husband whose own career keeps overlapping with hers. Screwball marital comedy welded onto a competence procedural, and the weld holds.

In Georgetown, a film actress watches her twelve-year-old daughter deteriorate through every test American medicine can offer, until the only people left to call are two priests. Friedkin shoots it as a procedural about institutions failing, which is why the religious material still bites.

Two New York narcotics detectives work a hunch about a Brooklyn nightclub owner into a surveillance operation on a French heroin shipment, mostly by standing about in the cold. The famous chase was shot in live traffic, and the film is strikingly unbothered about whether its hero is a good man.

A thoroughly selfish woman dies, is admitted to a perfectly designed afterlife by clerical error, and sets about earning her place by studying moral philosophy with a professor who is also dead. A network sitcom that actually teaches ethics, and rebuilds its own premise more often than any comedy should survive.

Home from university with no plans and a swimming pool to stare at, a young man drifts into an affair with a friend's wife and then falls for her daughter. Nichols frames alienation better than almost anyone, and the film is colder about its hero than its reputation as a romance suggests.

Five adult siblings, scattered and damaged, are pulled back to the summer in a decaying mansion that killed their mother, in timelines that keep cutting into each other. Flanagan is more interested in inherited grief than in ghosts, and the family drama would stand up without them.

A boy in 1950s Maine finds a fifty-foot metal machine eating the local power lines and hides it from a federal agent convinced it is a Soviet weapon. Bird made a Cold War film for children about choosing what you are, and the restraint of the last twenty minutes is remarkable.

A New York property heir linked to three deaths across three decades agrees to sit for filmed interviews with the director who dramatised his story, over several years. The first run is built almost entirely on letting a subject talk; the belated second series is thinner and taken with its own legend.

Five mismatched crooks rent a room from an elderly widow in a lopsided house above King's Cross, posing as a string quintet while they plan a robbery. Ealing at its blackest: the whole joke is that the sweet old lady is the immovable object.

Unreleased footage of the Chicago Bulls' 1997-98 season, shot by a crew given full access to the locker room, cut against the whole arc of Michael Jordan's career. Superb archive, but Jordan's own company had final say, and the series settles his old scores rather than examining them.

A thuggish enforcer and an incompetent private investigator are pushed into working together on a missing girl in 1977 Los Angeles, and keep stumbling into a pornography case tied to the car industry. Black writes the best two-hander dialogue in the business, and Gosling plays panic better than anyone expected.

In a curtained house on Jersey at the end of the war, a tense mother keeps her two photosensitive children out of the light and waits for a husband who has not come home, when three servants arrive. Old-fashioned in the best way: no gore, everything built from doors, fog and withheld information.

A Gotham mob driver with a limp and an eye for a gap moves on the vacuum left by the Falcone family's collapse, while the heir who spent a decade in Arkham comes back to claim it. Played as a straight seventies crime saga rather than a superhero show, and Farrell vanishes under the prosthetics.

One long shift in a Pittsburgh emergency department, an hour per episode in real time, following a senior attending still carrying the pandemic and the residents he is meant to be teaching. The real-time structure sounds like a gimmick and instead makes the triage arithmetic almost unbearable.

A young dancer is taken into an imperious impresario's company, given the lead in a new ballet, and then made to choose between the man she loves and the work. The fifteen-minute ballet sequence remains the most ambitious thing in British film; around it sits a cold, exact tragedy.

Twenty-five years on, a retired Buenos Aires court investigator writes a novel about the rape and murder case that broke him, reopening the file and his feelings for his former boss at once. The romance is the engine rather than the padding, and one unbroken shot into a football stadium is justly famous.

A knight home from the Crusades plays chess with Death on a plague-struck Swedish shore, stalling for time enough to get one straight answer about God. Far earthier and funnier than its reputation suggests, and the troupe of travelling players matter as much as the theology.

The new head of a flailing Hollywood studio spends his days trying to protect the films he loves from the business he now runs, and makes things worse at every turn. Shot in long unbroken takes that turn each meeting into a slow-motion collision.

A bamboo cutter finds a tiny girl inside a stalk, raises her as a princess, and watches her chafe against every gilded thing he buys for her. Takahata leaves the charcoal and watercolour deliberately unfinished, so the drawing itself carries the grief.

Five young people drive into the Texas heat to check on a family grave and stop at the wrong farmhouse. Almost bloodless, and worse for it: the horror lives in the sound design, the sunstroke light and one unbearable dinner.

When her cyclist grandson is kidnapped mid-Tour de France, an unstoppable old woman and her enormous dog follow the trail to a grotesque American city. Nearly wordless, drawn with a caricaturist's cruelty, and held together by a music-hall trio who refuse to be pitied.

A devout Scottish policeman flies to a remote island to investigate a missing girl and finds a community that has cheerfully abandoned Christianity. The folk songs do the work a monster would do elsewhere - sunlit, catchy and entirely sincere.

Stranded on an island with no humans left to serve, a shipwrecked service robot ends up raising an orphaned gosling she cannot at first understand. DreamWorks going painterly - the animation looks brushed rather than rendered, and the film is unusually honest about letting go.

A Puritan family, banished from their plantation, farm a plot at the edge of a New England wood and begin losing children and blaming one another. Much of the dialogue is lifted from period records, which is why the paranoia lands harder than the scares.

In Oslo, a woman approaching thirty keeps swapping careers and partners, less from cruelty than from a suspicion that the right life is one decision away. Told in twelve chapters, and clear-eyed about the damage ordinary indecision does to other people.

Three nineteen-year-olds discover in 1980 that they are identical triplets separated at birth, and the film follows them from talk-show novelty act to the research programme that arranged the split. It turns from delight to anger about halfway through, and never pretends otherwise.

A booming, perpetually aggrieved stage actor takes voiceover work he despises while his career and love life run aground in ever more surreal ways. Berry's delivery is the whole engine; the plotting is nonsense by design and the recording-booth scenes are the best of it.

Two British climbers summit a Peruvian peak in 1985 and one breaks his leg on the descent, forcing his partner into a decision about the rope. The men narrate their own reconstruction, which is why it grips even when you already know how it ended.

A cowboy doll who has always been his owner's favourite finds himself demoted when a deluded space ranger action figure arrives. The first fully computer-animated feature, and it still works because the jealousy is real and half the jokes are aimed at the parents.

A dismembered torso surfaces in the harbour of an isolated Icelandic fjord town just as a ferry docks and a blizzard seals the roads, leaving the local police chief with everyone still inside. Unhurried Nordic crime carried by Ólafur Darri Ólafsson's bulk and patience; later seasons move inland and lose some of the claustrophobia.

Dying of kidney failure, a Thai farmer retires to the countryside, where the ghost of his wife and a son who became a forest spirit turn up to sit with him. Unhurried to the point of trance, with reincarnation handled as a matter of household routine.

A small robot has spent centuries compacting rubbish on an abandoned Earth when a sleek probe arrives hunting for plant life, and he is immediately besotted. The near-silent first act is the finest thing Pixar has made; what follows is broader and more conventional.

An inventor and his silent dog take in a lodger to cover the bills, and the penguin who moves in has designs on a pair of remote-controlled techno-trousers. Thirty minutes of plasticine engineered like a heist thriller, with a model-railway chase that is still the best action sequence Aardman has built.

Realising he has no memory of his own part in the 1982 Lebanon war, an Israeli veteran tracks down former comrades to reconstruct what he did there. An animated documentary in the literal sense: real interviews, drawn so that memory and hallucination share a frame.

At 2:17 one morning, seventeen children from the same class get out of bed, walk out of their front doors and disappear, and the town decides their teacher is to blame. Told in overlapping chapters from different residents, which keeps the mystery honest; the comedy underneath does more work than the scares.

Two street gangs, one Puerto Rican and one white, fight over a few blocks of Manhattan while a boy from each side falls for the other's girl. Robbins's choreography still looks startling; the brownface make-up and dubbed singing voices have aged very badly.

In a decaying Staten Island house, four vampire flatmates bicker over chores and centuries-old grudges while a documentary crew they mostly ignore keeps filming. Broader than the film that spawned it and better for it - the energy vampire alone justifies the spin-off.

Footage shot in Kinshasa in 1974, where Ali fought Foreman and a three-day soul festival ran alongside the bout, sat unreleased for two decades before becoming this film. Less about boxing than about Ali inventing himself in public, and the contemporaneous interviews carry it.

A green-skinned student at a school for wizards is roomed with the most popular girl in it, and a friendship forms that Oz will later have to explain away. Chu stages the show big and sincere; Erivo's voice does more heavy lifting than the plot.

Six unconnected Argentinian stories about people who stop absorbing an insult and escalate instead: a road-rage feud, a hit-and-run, a wedding reception coming apart. Anthology films usually sag somewhere; this one gets meaner and funnier as it goes.

An Indian guru's followers buy a ranch in rural Oregon in 1981, build a city on it, and escalate a fight with their neighbours into wiretapping, immigration fraud and mass poisoning. Assembled from the commune's own tapes, and careful to let both sides be sympathetic and appalling by turns.

Two unemployed actors at the fag end of the 1960s flee a squalid Camden flat for a Lake District cottage belonging to one of their uncles, and are catastrophically unequipped for the countryside. Endlessly quotable, but it is the melancholy under the drinking that gives it a second life.

Sent to help exterminate the last wolves outside seventeenth-century Kilkenny, a hunter's daughter meets a wild girl whose spirit leaves her body at night. Cartoon Saloon draw with the pencil lines left in, and switch style entirely between the ruled town and the forest.

Two Mexico City teenagers talk an older woman into a road trip to a beach they have invented, and spend the drive lying to each other about sex. A narrator keeps interrupting with facts about the country outside the car, which is the film's real subject.

A newly appointed cabinet minister arrives wanting to change things and meets a permanent secretary whose entire craft is ensuring nothing changes. Written off the back of civil-service sources, and the jokes still work as load-bearing descriptions of how Whitehall operates.

Across a year bracketed by a wedding and a funeral, a Taipei family drift: a disillusioned engineer, his teenage daughter, his small son photographing the backs of people's heads. Three hours that never feel long, because Yang lets ordinary scenes run until they turn.

A country girl and a Tokyo boy start waking up in each other's bodies without warning, leaving notes to negotiate lives they cannot control. The body-swap comedy is a set-up for something else entirely, and the swerve is handled better than the exposition that follows it.
